title: Keeping Up with AI When the Classroom Is the Frontier
author: Marc Watkins
summary: Watkins asks how educators can stay informed about AI without becoming siloed when the technology changes faster than understanding. He notes that about half of American adults use chatbots while the rest barely do, so people debate very different realities. Product churn compounds the problem: OpenAI is retiring CustomGPTs and Prism, joining Sora and Atlas, so classroom tools and bespoke platforms built on earlier features can vanish within months. He explains that agentic workflows, which run autonomous loops with tools, behave differently from quick 'flash' chat answers, and that people's stance on AI often rests on weaker free models. Drawing on Han Lee's Mario-based explainer and developer critiques by Appleton and Wattenberger, he describes his own weekly agent workflow that gathers and sorts AI news into a shareable sheet and a monthly newsletter, with transparent disclosure of what the agent did versus his role. He closes by prioritizing curiosity, creativity and comfort with uncertainty in students, and by designing on-ramps and off-ramps so people can choose their level of AI use. The setting is higher education but the lessons apply to schools.
points: Half of adults rarely use AI, so public debate is split between people encountering very different capabilities; informing yourself on current tools matters even if you do not adopt them.
Rapid retirement of features such as CustomGPTs means classroom tools and custom chatbots built on them are fragile, so plan for change rather than lock in.
Agentic and flash-model outputs differ in quality, and judging AI from free, fast models understates what advanced agentic systems can do.
Watkins shows a practical agent workflow (weekly web search sorted into a spreadsheet, a monthly curated newsletter) while insisting on transparent disclosure of what AI did and what he did.
Offer on-ramps and off-ramps: curiosity about AI need not equal fluency with a product, and choice should not default to the newest tool.
quotes: AI may not be inevitable, but for many, it has already happened, and that’s caused a lot of problems.
In education, if you take the time to develop something and integrate it, you don’t expect it to disappear or radically change months later!

We’re going to need to develop a social contract around AI and its place in our world. In order to do that, we have to figure out a way to stay informed about AI and talk to one another about it, not past each other.
Agents operate in autonomous loops, using tools to look up information, code interactives, and use machine reasoning to check and recheck responses.

This matters because your engagement with AI often informs your stance on it, and if your main interaction with AI is through freemium models, or not at all, then you likely struggle to understand what the actual capabilities are of more advanced agentic systems currently on the market.
At its core is a design problem. Developers have optimized interfaces for agentic tasks, where human review and interaction is often considered ancillary, when it should be centered on that dynamic.
If someone read a disclosure note and came up to you and asked how you used AI, would you be able to articulate what your role was vs. an agent?
I also don’t believe that curiosity about AI needs to equal fluency with an AI tool or product

Having on-ramps and off-ramps that allow people to choose their comfort level with AI will continue to be a meaningful design decision for me, because choice should matter and not always default to the newest shiny thing as the norm.
